blocks.content: 1. DNS Load Balancing: A Different Layer Entirely
blocks.text: 1. DNS Load Balancing: A Different Layer Entirely

blocks.content: Most load balancers sit in the infrastructure between the client and the servers, watching live traffic and routing each request. DNS load balancing works completely differently: it acts before the request ever even leaves the client's machine, at the domain name resolution step, returning multiple possible IP addresses for one domain and letting the client pick one.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274300920-872535040.png
blocks.alt: DNS load balancing operates a full step earlier than any application load balancer ever sees a request

blocks.content: 2. How DNS Resolution Works

Before a browser can connect to api.MyDSA, it needs an actual IP address, and that lookup is DNS resolution. DNS load balancing plugs directly into this flow to return different IPs to different clients.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274302857-153019431.png
blocks.alt: Every layer in this chain is a chance to serve a cached answer or route the client to a different server entirely

blocks.content: ["Browser cache: if the domain was resolved recently and the TTL hasn't expired, the browser reuses the cached IP with no DNS query at all","Resolver: usually the ISP's DNS server or a public resolver like 8.8.8.8, which also checks its own cache before doing any real lookup","Authoritative server: this is your actual DNS server, Route 53, Cloudflare DNS, or similar, and this is exactly where the load balancing logic lives, deciding which IP or IPs to hand back","Response: the client connects directly to whichever IP it received, the DNS server is completely out of the picture from this point on"]
items: Browser cache: if the domain was resolved recently and the TTL hasn't expired, the browser reuses the cached IP with no DNS query at all
Resolver: usually the ISP's DNS server or a public resolver like 8.8.8.8, which also checks its own cache before doing any real lookup
Authoritative server: this is your actual DNS server, Route 53, Cloudflare DNS, or similar, and this is exactly where the load balancing logic lives, deciding which IP or IPs to hand back
Response: the client connects directly to whichever IP it received, the DNS server is completely out of the picture from this point on

blocks.content: 3. TTL: The Most Important DNS Concept
blocks.text: 3. TTL: The Most Important DNS Concept

blocks.content: Every DNS record carries a TTL, time to live, measured in seconds. Once a client resolves an IP and caches it, that client won't ask again until the TTL expires. This single number is DNS load balancing's biggest limitation, changes never propagate instantly, only as fast as the TTL allows.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274304477-145554765.png
blocks.alt: TTL is a direct dial between cost and how quickly a change or failure actually reaches users

blocks.content: {"headers":["TTL Setting","Effect"],"rows":[["High (e.g. 3600s)","Clients cache the IP for a long time. If a server goes down, users keep hitting the dead IP until the TTL finally expires, slow failover"],["Low (e.g. 30s)","Clients refresh DNS frequently. If a server fails, a new IP is picked up quickly, fast failover"]]}

blocks.title: The Real Tradeoff
blocks.content: High TTL means fewer DNS queries, better performance, and lower cost. Low TTL means faster recovery from a failure, at the cost of more DNS queries and more load on the DNS infrastructure itself.
4. DNS Record Types Relevant to Load Balancing
blocks.text: 4. DNS Record Types Relevant to Load Balancing

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274306095-286485588.png
blocks.alt: Which record type a domain uses shapes what load-balancing tricks are even possible for it

blocks.content: ["A record: maps a domain directly to an IPv4 address, the simplest and most common building block for every strategy in this topic","AAAA record: the same idea for IPv6 addresses, used identically to an A record wherever IPv6 is supported","CNAME: points a domain to another domain name instead of an IP directly, useful for pointing a subdomain at a third-party service without hardcoding its IP","ALIAS (or ANAME, provider-specific naming): behaves like a CNAME but is usable at the bare root domain, where a real CNAME is not legally allowed"]
items: A record: maps a domain directly to an IPv4 address, the simplest and most common building block for every strategy in this topic
AAAA record: the same idea for IPv6 addresses, used identically to an A record wherever IPv6 is supported
CNAME: points a domain to another domain name instead of an IP directly, useful for pointing a subdomain at a third-party service without hardcoding its IP
ALIAS (or ANAME, provider-specific naming): behaves like a CNAME but is usable at the bare root domain, where a real CNAME is not legally allowed

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274307652-195926829.png
blocks.alt: The DNS specification forbids a CNAME at the root domain, which is exactly the gap ALIAS records were invented to close

blocks.content: This last point matters more than it looks: the DNS specification does not allow a CNAME record at a domain's bare root, for example MyDSA itself rather than www.MyDSA, because the root also needs to carry other record types like MX for mail, which CNAME's rules forbid coexisting with. ALIAS-style records, offered by Route 53 and several other providers under their own names, exist specifically to let a root domain still point at a load-balanced target, like a CDN or another load balancer, without hardcoding a specific IP that could change.
5. Simple Round Robin DNS

The DNS server returns multiple A records for the same domain. Clients typically pick the first one in the list, and different clients receive the list in a different rotation order, so traffic naturally spreads across the available IPs. There is no health checking here at all, no intelligence, just multiple IPs in rotation.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274309291-446265344.png
blocks.alt: Round robin DNS keeps handing out a dead IP for as long as the TTL says clients should trust it

blocks.content: Example: Client 1 connects to 54.12.10.1, Client 2 connects to 54.12.10.2, Client 3 connects to 54.12.10.3, the DNS server simply rotates the order of the same three IPs in each response. If 54.12.10.2 goes down, DNS keeps returning it anyway, clients that resolve to that dead IP get errors until their TTL expires and they re-resolve to a different one.
6. Health Checks: How DNS Even Knows a Server Is Down
blocks.text: 6. Health Checks: How DNS Even Knows a Server Is Down

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274310856-77806154.png
blocks.alt: A DNS health check works the same way any other health check does, poll it, and stop trusting it if it stops answering correctly

blocks.content: Every routing strategy that reacts to failure, failover routing from section 11, and the multi-value answer routing covered next, depends on the DNS provider actually knowing which endpoints are healthy. A health checker, run by the DNS provider itself, periodically polls each configured endpoint, typically expecting an HTTP 200 response within a set time limit, and marks an endpoint unhealthy after enough consecutive failures, excluding it from future answers until it recovers.

This is exactly the mechanism failover routing relies on to detect that a primary should be abandoned, and it is precisely what plain round robin DNS from section 5 is missing entirely, which is why round robin alone keeps returning a dead IP indefinitely.
7. Multi-Value Answer Routing: Fixing Round Robin's Blind Spot
blocks.text: 7. Multi-Value Answer Routing: Fixing Round Robin's Blind Spot

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274312605-287070532.png
blocks.alt: Combining rotation with real health checks turns plain round robin into something that actually reacts to a failure

blocks.content: Multi-value answer routing is a distinct DNS routing policy that directly patches round robin DNS's biggest weakness. Instead of blindly rotating through every configured IP regardless of health, the DNS provider runs health checks against each one and returns only the healthy IPs, rotated, typically up to 8 per response.

This means a dead server configured behind multi-value answer routing stops appearing in DNS responses once its health check fails, clients simply never receive that IP anymore, rather than receiving it and having to fail and retry as plain round robin DNS would force them to do. It is not full load-based balancing the way an application load balancer provides, but it closes the specific, glaring gap section 5 identifies in the most basic approach.
8. Latency-Based Routing

The DNS server measures network latency between different regions or data centers and the client's resolver, then returns the IP of whichever server currently has the lowest latency for that specific client.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024506-873989514.png
blocks.alt: The DNS server picks the genuinely fastest region for this specific client, not a fixed geographic assignment

blocks.content: Example: a Mumbai user's latency to us-east-1 measures 280ms, while their latency to ap-south-1 measures only 12ms, so DNS returns ap-south-1's IP, since it has the lower latency for that user right now. This directly improves user experience by routing to whichever region is actually fastest, not necessarily the nearest one geographically.
9. Geolocation Routing

Routes requests based on the physical location of the client's DNS resolver, not measured latency, physical location specifically. All Indian users can be routed to a Mumbai server, all EU users to Frankfurt, all US users to Virginia, regardless of which of those happens to be technically fastest for any individual user.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274316242-573125826.png
blocks.alt: Geolocation routing is a fixed, deliberate assignment by region rather than a measurement of speed

blocks.content: Example: a user in India always goes to ap-south-1, even if another region happens to be genuinely faster for them at that moment. Use cases include GDPR and data residency requirements, legal restrictions or geo-blocking, and serving language or otherwise localized content specific to a region.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274317877-736926924.png
blocks.alt: The two routing strategies solve genuinely different problems and are chosen for different reasons

blocks.content: {"headers":["Routing Type","Decided By","Used For"],"rows":[["Geolocation Routing","Fixed region assignment","Compliance and control, for example data residency law"],["Latency-Based Routing","Real-time measured speed","Performance, always finding the genuinely fastest region"]]}
10. Weighted Routing

Each DNS record is assigned a weight, and the DNS provider distributes traffic proportionally across them. A record with weight 80 receives roughly 80% of traffic, one with weight 20 receives roughly 20%. This is exactly how canary deployments and blue-green deployments can be implemented at the DNS level itself.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274319576-92525747.png
blocks.alt: Weighted routing turns a deployment rollout into a simple, adjustable traffic-split ratio

blocks.content: Example: 90% of users go to Server v1 while 10% go to Server v2, useful for gradual rollouts like canary releases or A/B testing, where the weight can simply be dialed up over time as confidence in the new version grows.
11. Failover Routing

One server is designated primary, another secondary. DNS always returns the primary's IP under normal conditions. If the primary starts failing health checks, DNS automatically switches to returning the secondary's IP instead. This is disaster recovery, not everyday load balancing, traffic goes to the backup only once the primary is actually down.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396024505-403017560.png
blocks.alt: DNS keeps returning the primary until health checks confirm it has actually failed, then switches automatically

blocks.content: Normal operation: DNS returns the primary, for example 54.12.10.1. After roughly 30 seconds of consecutive health check failures, DNS begins returning the secondary instead, for example 54.12.10.2, until the primary recovers.
12. DNS Load Balancing vs Application Load Balancing
blocks.text: 12. DNS Load Balancing vs Application Load Balancing

blocks.content: DNS load balancing and application load balancers, Nginx, AWS ALB, and similar, are not competing alternatives, they operate at genuinely different layers and are almost always used together in a real production system.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274322712-782067235.png
blocks.alt: DNS answers which region, an application load balancer answers which specific server within that region

blocks.content: A typical production system uses both: DNS routes users to the right region first, and once inside that region, an application load balancer distributes the request across the individual servers actually running there.
13. How They Work Together: A Concrete Walkthrough
blocks.text: 13. How They Work Together: A Concrete Walkthrough

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396019242-484857628.png
blocks.alt: Five steps, spanning two entirely different load-balancing layers, for a single request

blocks.content: ["Step 1, user request starts: the user hits the domain, for example api.MyDSA, which goes first to Route 53, DNS, not directly to any server","Step 2, Route 53 decides the region: Route 53 checks latency from the user's location to the available regions, choosing ap-south-1 if the user is closer to India, or us-east-1 if closer to the US, this is latency-based routing from section 8","Step 3, DNS returns the ALB endpoint: Route 53 responds with the IP or endpoint of the nearest Application Load Balancer, and the client sends its actual request there","Step 4, the ALB handles regional traffic: the selected ALB receives the request and distributes it across the servers within that region, Server 1, Server 2, and so on, using algorithms like round robin or least connections from the Load Balancing Algorithms topic","Step 5, health checks and failover at both layers: if an entire region becomes slow or unreachable, Route 53 can redirect traffic to a different, healthy region; if a single server inside one region fails, the ALB alone handles that, routing around it without Route 53 ever needing to be involved"]
items: Step 1, user request starts: the user hits the domain, for example api.MyDSA, which goes first to Route 53, DNS, not directly to any server

Step 2, Route 53 decides the region: Route 53 checks latency from the user's location to the available regions, choosing ap-south-1 if the user is closer to India, or us-east-1 if closer to the US, this is latency-based routing from section 8
Step 3, DNS returns the ALB endpoint: Route 53 responds with the IP or endpoint of the nearest Application Load Balancer, and the client sends its actual request there

Step 4, the ALB handles regional traffic: the selected ALB receives the request and distributes it across the servers within that region, Server 1, Server 2, and so on, using algorithms like round robin or least connections from the Load Balancing Algorithms topic

Step 5, health checks and failover at both layers: if an entire region becomes slow or unreachable, Route 53 can redirect traffic to a different, healthy region; if a single server inside one region fails, the ALB alone handles that, routing around it without Route 53 ever needing to be involved

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274326021-769287821.png
blocks.alt: Failover happens at exactly the layer where the failure actually occurred, a whole region or just one server

blocks.content: Route 53 answers which region. The ALB answers which server. Neither layer needs to know how the other one makes its decision, and that separation is exactly what makes the combination powerful.

The example below implements four of the routing strategies from sections 5, 8, 10, and 11 directly: round robin cycling through a fixed IP list, weighted routing selecting proportionally to assigned weights, latency-based routing picking the genuinely fastest region, and failover routing switching to the secondary only once the primary is marked unhealthy.
Worked Example 1: A Global SaaS Rollout
blocks.text: Worked Example 1: A Global SaaS Rollout

blocks.content: A SaaS product serving customers across India, Europe, and the US uses Route 53 with latency-based routing across three regional deployments. A European customer's request first hits Route 53, which measures latency and returns eu-central-1's ALB endpoint, since it consistently beats both other regions for that customer. The ALB in that region then load-balances the request across its own pool of application servers using least connections.

During a new version's rollout, the team adds weighted routing within eu-central-1 specifically: 95% of traffic continues to the stable v1 deployment, 5% goes to the new v2 canary. TTL for these records is deliberately kept low, 60 seconds, specifically during the rollout window, so that if v2 needs to be pulled entirely, that change propagates to nearly all clients within a minute rather than sitting cached for an hour.
Worked Example 2: A Small Startup's First DR Setup
blocks.text: Worked Example 2: A Small Startup's First DR Setup

blocks.content: A startup running a single-region deployment wants basic disaster recovery without the cost of full multi-region latency-based routing. They configure failover routing from section 11: a primary record pointing at their main region, and a secondary pointing at a minimal, low-cost standby deployment in a different region, with a health check polling the primary every 30 seconds.

Under normal operation, every client resolves to the primary. If the primary region suffers an extended outage, DNS begins returning the secondary's IP once the health check confirms enough consecutive failures, and the standby, though smaller and not meant for full production load, keeps the product minimally reachable while the primary is repaired. This is deliberately not multi-value answer routing from section 7, that would spread load across both regions during normal operation, here the standby should never receive production traffic except during a genuine failure.
Common Mistakes

["Relying on round robin DNS alone for a production system that genuinely needs health-aware failover, since round robin DNS has no health checking whatsoever","Setting a high TTL on records that need to support fast failover, then being surprised recovery takes as long as the TTL itself","Confusing geolocation routing with latency-based routing, and using a fixed regional assignment when the actual goal was finding the fastest region dynamically","Treating DNS load balancing and an application load balancer as competing choices instead of complementary layers that solve different problems","Reaching for a CNAME at a domain's bare root and discovering the DNS specification forbids it, instead of using an ALIAS-style record from the start","Confusing multi-value answer routing with failover routing, one spreads load across several healthy endpoints at once, the other reserves a standby for use only during an actual outage"]
items: Relying on round robin DNS alone for a production system that genuinely needs health-aware failover, since round robin DNS has no health checking whatsoever
Setting a high TTL on records that need to support fast failover, then being surprised recovery takes as long as the TTL itself
Confusing geolocation routing with latency-based routing, and using a fixed regional assignment when the actual goal was finding the fastest region dynamically
Treating DNS load balancing and an application load balancer as competing choices instead of complementary layers that solve different problems
Reaching for a CNAME at a domain's bare root and discovering the DNS specification forbids it, instead of using an ALIAS-style record from the start
Confusing multi-value answer routing with failover routing, one spreads load across several healthy endpoints at once, the other reserves a standby for use only during an actual outage

blocks.content: Practice

A global video platform needs to route EU users to Frankfurt specifically for GDPR compliance, regardless of whether another region might be technically faster for some of those users. Using sections 8 and 9, explain which DNS routing strategy fits this requirement and why the alternative would be the wrong choice here.

A team is about to roll out a risky new backend version and wants the ability to instantly roll back to 0% traffic if something goes wrong. Using sections 3 and 10, explain what TTL setting you would choose during the rollout window and why, and how weighted routing would be adjusted at each stage of the rollout.

A small team wants a domain's bare root, not a subdomain, to point at a load-balanced target that could change IPs over time. Using section 4, explain why a plain CNAME record cannot be used here and what type of record actually solves it.

Using sections 5 and 7, explain concretely why a system using multi-value answer routing recovers from one server going down faster than a system using plain round robin DNS, even though both return multiple IPs.
Key Takeaways

DNS load balancing operates a full layer earlier than any application load balancer, at name resolution itself, returning different IPs to different clients before a single request is even sent. TTL is the central lever controlling this entire layer, trading query cost and performance against how fast a change or failure actually reaches users.

Round robin, latency-based, geolocation, weighted, and failover routing each solve a genuinely different problem, and DNS load balancing is never a replacement for an application load balancer, the two work together, DNS deciding which region, an application load balancer deciding which server within that region. The next topics in this module, Anycast Routing and Global vs Regional Load Balancers, build directly on this same regional-routing foundation.
